title: Borobudur built
hook: in Java, a stone mountain of a monument, carved with the life and the Jataka

segments.voice: Yesterday, Luang Prabang's dawn: rice placed in silence into each bowl. Your line was the line at dawn. Did you give one small thing quietly, asking nothing back? Today we cross the sea to Java. Day eight hundred ninety.

From a distance, across the green fields of central Java, in Indonesia, it looks like a hill that someone has tidied. Gray stone stacked in terraces, one on top of the next, narrowing as it rises, with a crown of bell-shaped stupas on top and volcanoes behind it. Walk closer and the stone turns into pictures. Panel after panel, wall after wall: a prince in a palace, a woman asleep, a forest hermit, a hare by a fire, ships at sea. There is no hall to step into out of the sun. The whole thing is meant to be walked. Today, how Borobudur was built, and what its builders carved into it.
screen: `A HILL OF TERRACES IN JAVA.` → `THE STONE TURNS INTO PICTURES.` → `NO HALL INSIDE. YOU WALK IT.`

segments.voice: First, the shape. Borobudur is a stupa, a monument of the kind we met at Sanchi and Shwedagon. But its builders raised it over a natural hill, wrapping the hill in stone, terrace above terrace, so that the stupa became a mountain you can climb. There is no room inside to gather in. The monument itself is the path. Second, the life of the Buddha in stone. Along the walls of one gallery, carved panels tell his story in order: the prince in the palace, the sights that troubled him, leaving home, the years of seeking, the awakening, the first teaching. Scholars match these panels to a Sanskrit telling of the life called the Lalitavistara. Third, the lives before that life. Other panels carve the Jataka, the stories of the Buddha's past births as an animal, a king, a merchant, a hermit. In one story, a hare who has nothing to offer a hungry traveler but himself leaps into the fire. Stories like these teach the long patience it takes to grow a bodhisattva's heart, one life at a time. Fourth, the stone is a book you read with your feet. The panels run in order around each terrace, so a pilgrim reads them by walking around the monument with it on the right, the way stupas are circled in respect, and climbs a terrace only after finishing the story below. Nobody hurries Borobudur. You read it slowly or you don't read it at all. Tomorrow we'll make the climb itself, all the way to the top.
screen: `A STUPA BUILT OVER A HILL.` · `THE BUDDHA'S LIFE, PANEL BY PANEL.` · `THE JATAKA: LIVES BEFORE THAT LIFE.` · `A BOOK YOU READ WITH YOUR FEET.` · then, large: `A MOUNTAIN OF STONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture the great terraces. Close your eyes and stand at the foot of Borobudur in the early light. Gray stone rising in steps above you. Mist on the fields behind. Let your eyes travel up, terrace by terrace, to the stupas on top. Then come back down to the first wall, to a single carved panel at eye level. Look at it the way you'd look at a picture in a children's book: one figure, one gesture, one moment. Stay there, breathing. The bell holds the time.
Borobudur built. A stupa raised over a hill in Java, terrace on terrace, carved with the Buddha's life and his past lives, meant to be read by walking. Today's word.
Your line: a mountain of stone. Today, when something feels too big to finish, look at just one panel of it, one small piece, and do that. Day eight hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Buddhist pilgrims, especially at the Vesak festival, walk Borobudur's terraces clockwise, keeping the monument on their right, and the carved panels of the Buddha's life and past lives are read in order as they go.

notes: All paraphrased; nothing quoted. No dates, dynasty or panel counts given, under the claims rule.
'Raised over a natural hill': standard archaeological description; confirm.
Matching of the life panels to the Lalitavistara: standard identification for the first gallery's main wall; confirm wording ('scholars match').
The hare story is used as an example of a Jataka; its presence among Borobudur's reliefs (Jatakamala panels) should be confirmed, or the hook's 'a hare by a fire' changed.
Hook images (prince in a palace, woman asleep, hermit, ships) are general descriptions of the reliefs; the ship reliefs are well known. Confirm.
Reading order: clockwise circumambulation (pradakshina), terrace by terrace; confirm.
